title: UK rates respondents expected a November rise, but differed on how long 4¼% would last
summary: An October poll of UK rates-market participants placed an average probability of 86.0% on Bank Rate reaching 4% at the 5 November meeting. The result was released on 6 November. The responses therefore preserve what the panel expected before the decision, while the public release arrived after it. The Bank’s staff designed the questions without MPC members’ involvement. The 80 participating firms were selected for their involvement and expertise in UK rates and money markets or their engagement with the Bank. Their answers measure the expectations of that panel. They are neither MPC votes nor probabilities extracted from derivatives prices. Fieldwork took place on 21–23 October (survey introduction and question 1).

The median of respondents’ most likely Bank Rate outcomes was 4% for November and December and 4.25% from February through September 2027, and also one year ahead. It fell to 4% for the end of 2027, 3.5% two years ahead and 3.25% five years ahead. The interquartile range was exactly 4% for the November and December meetings. In February both outer quartiles were 4.25%. Dispersion reappeared further out, with the middle half spanning 4% to 4.5% for November 2027. These are percentiles taken separately at each date. Connecting the medians describes the centre of the published panel, but does not reconstruct the path any particular respondent expected to trade.

The probability questions show how a tight cluster of modal calls can conceal uncertainty. The 78 firms answering the distribution questions assigned an average 13.1% to 3.75% in November, against 86.0% for 4%, with only 0.8% above 4%. For December the weight on 4% declined to 71.9%, and 4.25% received 19.5%. A year ahead the two largest cells were 4.25% at 24.3% and 4% at 23.0%. Adding the published cells above 4% gives 53.7% for the year-ahead distribution, while about 23.2% lay below 4%. A median point forecast of 4.25% therefore coexisted with substantial probability on paths both above and below it. The survey did not publish the price of hedging those tails.

Energy and related commodities accounted for 30.3% of the mean weight respondents attached to near-term policy drivers. Realised non-energy inflation received 18.5%, domestic activity and the labour market 17.2%, forward-looking inflation indicators 16.4%, and MPC communication 15.3%. Asked how they treated the energy shock, 52 respondents assumed moderate extra wage or price effects, 17 assumed no new second-round effects and nine assumed stronger and more persistent ones. Six-month oil assumptions were concentrated in the 85–99 dollar range, selected by 46 respondents; 20 chose 100–114 dollars. For UK gas 29 selected 150–179 pence a therm and 23 chose 180–209. Each question reports aggregate responses separately. The tables do not identify whether the people expecting higher gas prices also expected the strongest wage response or the highest policy rate.

Conditional on their own Bank Rate paths, respondents’ median modal CPI forecast rose from 3.8% in late 2026 to 4.0% in the first quarter of 2027, then fell to 3.4% in the third quarter. The horizon medians were 3.0% at one year, 2.3% at two, 2.1% at three and 2.0% at five. The three-year inflation distribution still assigned 9.9% above 3%. For inflation averaged between five and ten years ahead, the corresponding probability was 8.7%, even though 38.2% lay in the 1.81–2.20% bracket. A forecast centred close to target and an upside tail are compatible. The GDP growth medians were 1.4% in 2026 and 1.3% in 2027 (question 2).

The subjective neutral Bank Rate was 3.5% at the median of 77 returns, with its lower and upper quartiles at 3.25% and 3.5%. Of 78 people assessing risks to their neutral estimate, 42 saw upside, 32 judged the risks balanced and four saw downside. Separately, 43 of 79 judged the current stance restrictive to some degree, 24 broadly neutral and 12 accommodative. These questions establish that a probable rate increase could coexist with perceptions that policy was already constraining demand. Subtracting medians from different responses cannot establish the policy gap for a typical individual.

Median expected gilt issuance was £250 billion in 2026–27 and £290 billion in 2027–28. The median ten-year gilt yield forecast moved from 5.25% at end-2026 to 4.93% at end-2027. One-year exchange-rate medians were 1.3400 US dollars per pound and 0.8400 pounds per euro. These answers came from separate questions. They permit comparisons with subsequent releases, without identifying a supply premium or a common respondent’s joint gilt and currency forecast (questions 3–4 and corresponding Excel tables).

questions.question: How much of any movement on decision day was genuinely new relative to the surveyed distribution?
questions.detail: Compare the 21–23 October fieldwork with an overnight-indexed forward curve sampled on those same dates, then with the final quote before the November announcement. A change between the fieldwork and the meeting could reflect new information accumulated in between. Separate the part of the actual rate decision outside the surveyed modal call from any movement at longer maturities. A difference between survey probabilities and traded pricing can also reflect risk compensation or the selected respondent pool.

questions.question: Did the panel revise the near-term peak because energy prices rose or because the inferred wage response changed?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the next survey using exactly the same horizon, energy bins and wording on second-round effects. Compare changes in gas and oil assumptions with movements in the wage-response distribution and in near-term versus three-year inflation forecasts. If energy assumptions change sharply while the three-year tails and wage judgments move little, the evidence points toward an altered direct shock. Without linked respondent records, an aggregate comparison cannot establish the transmission within firms.

questions.question: Can the fall in projected gilt yields coexist with rising expected issuance after accounting for the policy path?
questions.detail: Line up the forecast target dates and measure the contemporaneous forward curve, duration supplied and inflation compensation. The survey projects marginal medians across groups with different response counts. Comparing the subsequent ten-year yield only to the end-December median would combine forecast error with news about growth, inflation, issuance and balance-sheet policy. A useful check is whether subsequent revisions in expected issuance also shifted long yields relative to shorter policy-sensitive maturities.

limitation: The survey was fielded before the meeting and published afterwards. Participants’ probabilities are equally aggregated subjective answers. The public tables provide no respondent-level cross-tabulations or traded market-implied probabilities.
